_note: Generated by scripts/build-stock-rhythms.mjs — do not edit by hand. Each track has one step string per bar (velocity 0-3); bars load as chained pages. bpm is engine bpm (eighth-note pulse for 6/8 and 12/8); tempo is the felt pulse.

rhythms.name: Basic 8th-Note Rock
rhythms.description: The foundation of rock drumming: steady 8th notes on the hi-hat, kick on 1 and 3, snare backbeat on 2 and 4. Heard on countless AC/DC and classic-rock records.
rhythms.tip: Count "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &" out loud and lock your right hand to every count before adding kick and snare.

rhythms.name: Quarter-Note Hi-Hat Rock
rhythms.description: The simplest rock beat: hi-hat on every beat, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. A great first groove and a common choice for heavy, open-sounding choruses.
rhythms.tip: Notice that hand and foot hit together on every beat — keep them perfectly lined up so they sound like one note.

rhythms.name: Ride Cymbal Rock
rhythms.description: The basic rock beat moved from the hi-hat to the ride cymbal for a bigger, washier sound — the classic choice for loud choruses and guitar solos.
rhythms.tip: Play the ride on the body of the cymbal, a few inches in from the edge, so it rings without turning into a crash.

rhythms.name: Rock Ballad
rhythms.description: A slow, spacious rock beat for power ballads, with plenty of room between the notes. The fill rolls from snare to floor tom to set up the next section.
rhythms.tip: Slow tempos are harder than they look — let each backbeat ring fully and resist rushing the space between notes.

rhythms.name: Rock with Syncopated Kick
rhythms.description: The basic rock beat with an extra kick on the "and" of 3, giving the groove a push into beat 4. This is probably the most-played rock and pop beat of all time.
rhythms.tip: The extra kick lands with the hi-hat on "and" — say "1, 3-and" out loud while playing until it feels natural.

rhythms.name: Stomp-Stomp-Clap
rhythms.description: The stadium stomp: two kicks, one snare-and-clap, then a breath — repeated. Famously the backbone of a certain anthem heard at every sports arena.
rhythms.tip: Leave the rest after each clap completely empty — the silence is part of the groove.

rhythms.name: 16th-Note Hi-Hat Rock
rhythms.description: A busier rock feel with 16th notes on the hi-hat and a syncopated kick pattern. Common in mid-tempo rock and pop-rock where the groove needs extra drive.
rhythms.tip: Play the 16ths with one hand and accent each quarter note — keep the in-between notes light so the backbeat still cuts through.

rhythms.name: Floor-Tom Jungle Groove
rhythms.description: A tribal, rumbling groove where the floor tom replaces the hi-hat and the snare still cracks on 2 and 4. Heard in surf rock, garage rock and big arena intros.
rhythms.tip: Let the floor tom ring and play it with a relaxed, bouncing stroke — the doubles should sound even, not rushed.

rhythms.name: Four-on-the-Floor Rock
rhythms.description: Disco-rock: kick on every beat with open hi-hats on the "ands" for a danceable lift. A staple of dance-rock and indie bands that want the floor moving.
rhythms.tip: Open the hat on the "and" and close it with your foot exactly on the next beat, so the kick and the hat "chick" land together.

rhythms.name: Half-Time Rock
rhythms.description: The snare moves to beat 3 only, so a fast song suddenly feels twice as slow and heavy. A go-to trick for big rock choruses, bridges and breakdowns.
rhythms.tip: Keep the hi-hat 8ths steady at the full tempo — only the snare halves, which is what creates the heavy, spacious feel.

rhythms.name: Pop Four-on-the-Floor
rhythms.description: Kick on every beat, snare and clap on 2 and 4, 8th-note hats — the engine of modern dance-pop.
rhythms.tip: Keep the kick volume identical on all four beats; an uneven kick makes the whole groove wobble.

rhythms.name: Pop Half-Time Ballad
rhythms.description: The snare lands only on beat 3, giving a slow, emotional feel over a faster pulse. Common in modern pop ballads and big, spacious choruses.
rhythms.tip: Think of beat 3 as the "big moment" in each bar and let the snare ring with a full, relaxed stroke.

rhythms.name: Synth-Pop 8ths
rhythms.description: A clean, mechanical 80s-style beat with snare and clap layered on the backbeat and a kick that pushes the "and" of 2 — think drum-machine new wave.
rhythms.tip: Play it like a machine: every hat the same volume, no swing, no pushing or pulling the time.

rhythms.name: Driving Pop with Open Hats
rhythms.description: An energetic pop-rock beat with a driving kick and open hi-hats on the "and" of 2 and 4 that make the chorus lift.
rhythms.tip: Open the hat just enough for a short "tsss" and snap it shut on the following beat — too long and it turns to mush.

rhythms.name: Pop 16th-Note Groove
rhythms.description: A polished mid-tempo pop groove with 16th-note hats, a syncopated kick and quiet ghost notes around the backbeat.
rhythms.tip: Accent the 8th notes on the hat and keep the in-between 16ths and ghost notes very soft — that contrast is what makes it feel smooth.

rhythms.name: Punk 8th-Note Drive
rhythms.description: Fast, relentless 8th notes with a doubled kick — the straight-ahead sound of classic punk, heard all over Ramones-era records.
rhythms.tip: At fast tempos use a loose wrist and let the stick rebound; tension is the enemy of endurance.

rhythms.name: D-Beat
rhythms.description: The galloping hardcore-punk beat: kick on 1, then a quick kick-kick pickup on the "and" of 2 and beat 3, under washing crash or ride 8ths. The signature of crust punk and d-beat bands.
rhythms.tip: Feel the kick pattern as "boom — ba-boom" and keep the cymbal 8ths steady over it.

rhythms.name: Half-Time Metal with Double Kick
rhythms.description: Continuous 16th-note double kick under a heavy half-time snare on beat 3 — the crushing sound of modern metal breakdowns.
rhythms.tip: Keep both feet at the same volume; practise the 16ths on the kicks alone, slowly, until left and right sound identical.

rhythms.name: Punk Skank Beat
rhythms.description: Kick and snare alternate "oom-pah" style at high speed, with the hats riding on top — the bouncing polka-punk beat of skate punk and pop-punk.
rhythms.tip: Start at half speed and keep the kick-snare alternation perfectly even before pushing the tempo up.

rhythms.name: Thrash Double-Time Beat
rhythms.description: The classic thrash beat: kick on every beat, snare on every "and", with the crash or ride on the quarter notes. The engine behind 80s thrash metal.
rhythms.tip: Build speed gradually with a metronome — clean and steady at 150 is better than sloppy at 200.

rhythms.name: Country Two-Beat
rhythms.description: The "boom-chick" of classic country: kick on the strong beats where the bass plays, snare on the off-beats, felt in a brisk cut time.
rhythms.tip: Lock the kick to the bass player's root-fifth notes and keep the snare light and crisp.

rhythms.name: Folk Waltz
rhythms.description: The "oom-pah-pah" of a waltz: kick on 1, cross-stick on 2 and 3. Used in country ballads, folk songs and traditional dances.
rhythms.tip: Count "1-2-3, 1-2-3" and make beat 1 slightly stronger so the listener always knows where the bar starts.

rhythms.name: Polka
rhythms.description: A lively "oom-pah" dance: kick on each beat and snare on each off-beat, bright and bouncy. Heard in Central European folk music, Tex-Mex conjunto and at every beer hall.
rhythms.tip: Keep it light and bouncy — think of dancers hopping, not a heavy rock backbeat.

rhythms.name: Country Shuffle
rhythms.description: A bouncy, swung 8th-note groove with kick on 1 and 3 and snare on 2 and 4 — the dance-hall shuffle of honky-tonk and Western swing.
rhythms.tip: Say "dum-da, dum-da" with a lopsided long-short feel and match the hi-hat to it.

rhythms.name: Train Beat
rhythms.description: Constant 16th notes on the snare with accents on 2 and 4, imitating a chugging locomotive. Heard on classic Johnny Cash–style country and rockabilly records.
rhythms.tip: Play the unaccented notes low to the drum and lift the stick only for the accents — the quiet notes should whisper.

rhythms.name: Basic Shuffle
rhythms.description: The foundation of blues drumming: swung 8ths on the hi-hat with a backbeat on 2 and 4. You hear it behind countless 12-bar blues jams.
rhythms.tip: Say "TUM-ba TUM-ba" as you play the hats so the second note of each pair lands late, like the last note of a triplet.

rhythms.name: Blues Rock Straight 8ths
rhythms.description: A straight, heavy 8th-note groove for blues rock, with a quick snare-to-floor-tom fill at the end of the phrase. Think late-60s British blues rock.
rhythms.tip: Dig into the backbeat and keep the hi-hat steady; the fill should land you right back on beat 1.

rhythms.name: Slow 12/8 Blues
rhythms.description: A slow blues ballad feel: steady triplets on the hi-hat, kick on 1 and 3 and a heavy backbeat on 2 and 4. The classic sound of a slow minor blues.
rhythms.tip: Count "1-trip-let 2-trip-let" out loud and let the slow tempo breathe; do not rush the triplets.

rhythms.name: Chicago Jump Blues
rhythms.description: An up-tempo, swing-era blues: jazz ride pattern, quarter-note kick and a crisp backbeat. Heard in jump blues bands and Chicago blues clubs.
rhythms.tip: Keep the four kick notes light and even; let the ride and snare do the talking.

rhythms.name: Half-Time Shuffle
rhythms.description: A half-time shuffle with the backbeat on beat 3 only and ghost notes filling the middle triplet partials. Made famous by Bernard Purdie and adapted by Jeff Porcaro.
rhythms.tip: Practice hats and ghost notes alone first: the hands interlock so every triplet partial gets exactly one note.

rhythms.name: Rockabilly Train Beat
rhythms.description: A chugging snare-only groove with accents on 2 and 4, like a train rolling down the track. The engine of rockabilly and boogie-woogie.
rhythms.tip: Alternate hands on the snare and keep the unaccented notes soft so the pattern sounds like "chugga-CHUGGA".

rhythms.name: Texas Shuffle
rhythms.description: Both hands play the shuffle together: ride on top while the left hand shuffles on the snare with big accents on 2 and 4, over four-on-the-floor kick. The driving Texas blues sound heard behind players like Stevie Ray Vaughan (Chris Layton on drums).
rhythms.tip: Keep the snare ghost notes barely touching the head so the 2 and 4 accents jump out.

rhythms.name: Basic Swing Ride Pattern
rhythms.description: The essential "spang-a-lang" ride cymbal pattern with the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4. Every jazz drummer builds on this.
rhythms.tip: Sing "ding, ding-ga ding, ding-ga" and make 2 and 4 slightly louder on the ride to match the hi-hat.

rhythms.name: Jazz Ballad (Brush Style)
rhythms.description: A soft ballad pattern played on the snare, approximating a brush part: the right-hand brush taps a swung pattern with weight on 2 and 4 while the hi-hat foot keeps time.
rhythms.tip: Play as quietly as you can while staying even; with real brushes, add a circular left-hand sweep underneath.

rhythms.name: Jazz Two-Feel
rhythms.description: A relaxed two-feel where the bass plays half notes: soft kick on 1 and 3 and a cross-stick on 4. Often used on the head of a tune before the band switches to four.
rhythms.tip: Think in half notes and keep it laid back; the space is what makes it feel like a two.

rhythms.name: Swing with Feathered Kick
rhythms.description: The ride pattern with very soft quarter notes on the bass drum, "feathered" so they are felt more than heard. This is the classic big-band and small-group swing foundation.
rhythms.tip: Play the kick heel-down and barely let the beater touch the head; it should support the bass, not cover it.

rhythms.name: Afro 12/8 Jazz Feel
rhythms.description: The African 12/8 bell pattern played on the ride bell over a soft dotted-quarter kick pulse. Drummers like Art Blakey and Elvin Jones used this feel on modal and Afro-Cuban jazz tunes.
rhythms.tip: Learn the bell pattern by singing it first; once it is automatic, the kick and hi-hat will fall into place.

rhythms.name: Jazz Waltz
rhythms.description: Swing in 3/4: the ride plays "1, 2-and, 3" with the hi-hat foot on 2 and 3 and light snare comping. A staple of modern jazz waltzes.
rhythms.tip: Feel the bar as one big pulse rather than three separate beats, and keep the hi-hat foot steady.

rhythms.name: Medium Swing with Snare Comping
rhythms.description: Steady ride and hi-hat with the left hand "comping" short snare figures on the offbeats, ending with a kick "bomb" on the and of 4. This is how drummers converse with the soloist in medium swing.
rhythms.tip: Keep the ride and hi-hat locked no matter what the snare does; comping is decoration, the ride is the time.

rhythms.name: Up-Tempo Bebop
rhythms.description: A fast bebop feel: light ride pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, sparse snare comping and an occasional kick bomb. Inspired by the approach of Max Roach and Kenny Clarke.
rhythms.tip: Stay relaxed and play close to the cymbal; at fast tempos the swing flattens out, so do not force the triplet.

rhythms.name: Basic 16th-Note Funk
rhythms.description: The foundation of funk: one-hand 16th notes on the hi-hat, a solid backbeat, and a kick that bounces off beat 1. This is the starting point for almost every funk groove.
rhythms.tip: Accent the hat on each quarter note and keep the in-between 16ths light so the groove breathes.

rhythms.name: Funk with Ghost Notes
rhythms.description: Quiet ghost strokes on the snare fill the spaces between the backbeats, giving funk its greasy, rolling texture. Think of the classic James Brown-era drummers like Clyde Stubblefield.
rhythms.tip: Keep ghost notes just an inch off the head — they should be felt more than heard against the backbeat.

rhythms.name: Go-Go Pocket
rhythms.description: The swung, percolating groove of Washington D.C. go-go, driven by a lilting hi-hat, cowbell and congas. Chuck Brown and the Soul Searchers made it famous.
rhythms.tip: Let the swing pull the "a" of each beat late and relax — go-go sits deep in the pocket, never on top.

rhythms.name: Linear Funk
rhythms.description: In a linear groove no two limbs ever strike at the same time, creating a flowing, intricate 16th-note line. The style was popularised by players like David Garibaldi and Steve Gadd.
rhythms.tip: Play it slowly as one continuous 16th stream across the kit — every step should have exactly one sound.

rhythms.name: Open Hi-Hat Funk
rhythms.description: Opening the hi-hat on the "&" of 2 and 4 adds a sizzling lift that is all over funk and disco-funk records. The hat closes again on the next downbeat.
rhythms.tip: Close the hat with your foot exactly on the following beat so the open note sounds short and choked.

rhythms.name: Syncopated Kick Funk
rhythms.description: The kick dances around the beat on 16th-note offbeats while the snare holds the backbeat. Great for building independence between your foot and hands.
rhythms.tip: Count the 16ths out loud ("1-e-&-a") and lock each kick to its syllable before speeding up.

rhythms.name: 12/8 Soul Ballad
rhythms.description: A slow triplet-based feel with the backbeat on beats 2 and 4, used on classic soul and doo-wop ballads. Each beat is divided into three 8th notes.
rhythms.tip: Count "1-trip-let, 2-trip-let" and accent the first note of each group on the hi-hat.

rhythms.name: 60s Soul Backbeat
rhythms.description: A warm, simple soul beat with a strong backbeat and a kick that pushes into beat 3. You hear it all over Stax and Atlantic records, played by drummers like Al Jackson Jr.
rhythms.tip: Hit the backbeat with full, fat strokes and keep the hi-hat steady and even underneath.

rhythms.name: Motown Four-on-the-Snare
rhythms.description: The snare hits every quarter note, accenting 2 and 4, for the driving, danceable feel of 1960s Motown. Benny Benjamin anchored countless hits with this beat.
rhythms.tip: Keep beats 1 and 3 on the snare softer than the backbeats so the 2 and 4 still pop.

rhythms.name: R&B Slow Jam
rhythms.description: A laid-back, spacious groove for slow R&B and quiet-storm ballads. The space between notes is just as important as the notes themselves.
rhythms.tip: At slow tempos, resist rushing — let each backbeat land slightly late and ring out.

rhythms.name: Neo-Soul Lazy Pocket
rhythms.description: A swung, behind-the-beat feel with cross-stick backbeats and a loose, conversational kick. It is the sound of neo-soul drummers like Questlove and Chris Dave.
rhythms.tip: Think "drunk but in time" — relax every note a hair late while keeping the quarter-note pulse steady.

rhythms.name: New Jack Swing
rhythms.description: The late-80s fusion of R&B and hip-hop: heavily swung 16th hats, a snare-and-clap backbeat and a bouncy, syncopated kick. Teddy Riley is the style's chief architect.
rhythms.tip: Lean into the swing on the hi-hat — the "e" and "a" should feel like a shuffle, not straight 16ths.

rhythms.name: Boom Bap
rhythms.description: The classic 90s East Coast hip-hop beat: a heavy kick ("boom") and a cracking snare ("bap") with a lightly swung hi-hat. Producers like DJ Premier and Pete Rock defined the sound.
rhythms.tip: Hit the snare hard and the hats softly — boom bap lives on the contrast between them.

rhythms.name: Lo-Fi Hip-Hop
rhythms.description: A dusty, mellow, heavily swung beat at a relaxed tempo — the sound of study-beat playlists inspired by J Dilla and Nujabes.
rhythms.tip: Play everything softly and let the swing make the groove feel lazy and warm.

rhythms.name: Classic Breakbeat
rhythms.description: A sampled-funk-style break with a busy kick, ghosted snare pickups and a syncopated second half — the kind of drum break hip-hop was built on, in the spirit of the "Amen" and "Funky Drummer" breaks.
rhythms.tip: Lock the double kick at the start of each half of the bar before adding the ghost notes.

rhythms.name: Trap Half-Time
rhythms.description: Modern trap feels half-time: the snare and clap land only on beat 3 while the hi-hats skitter in 8ths and 16th-note bursts over a sparse 808-style kick.
rhythms.tip: Feel the pulse in half-time (one big beat per two clicks) and keep the hat bursts relaxed with your wrist.

rhythms.name: West Coast G-Funk
rhythms.description: The smooth, funk-sampled groove of 90s West Coast rap, with a snare-and-clap backbeat, a rolling kick and an open hat leading into the next bar. Dr. Dre's productions are the blueprint.
rhythms.tip: Keep the groove relaxed and bouncy — it should feel like cruising, never rushing.

rhythms.name: Basic Disco
rhythms.description: Four-on-the-floor kick, backbeat snare and the signature open hi-hat on every offbeat. This is the 1970s disco sound that later became the root of house music.
rhythms.tip: Open the hat on each "&" and snap it shut with your foot on the next beat for that "tss-tss" pulse.

rhythms.name: House
rhythms.description: The steady pulse of house music: a kick on every beat, claps on 2 and 4, and open hats on the offbeats, with closed hats filling the 16ths. Born in 1980s Chicago clubs.
rhythms.tip: Keep the kick perfectly even — in house, the four-on-the-floor is the heartbeat everything hangs on.

rhythms.name: Techno
rhythms.description: A driving, hypnotic four-on-the-floor with off-beat open hats and a ticking 16th-note hat pattern. It comes from Detroit and Berlin club culture.
rhythms.tip: Stay relentlessly consistent — techno is about repetition, so focus on identical, even strokes.

rhythms.name: Drum & Bass Two-Step
rhythms.description: The fast, rolling "two-step" of drum & bass: kick on 1 and the "&" of 3, snare on 2 and 4, at a breakneck tempo. It feels like a fast breakbeat over a half-time bassline.
rhythms.tip: Start at around 120 bpm and creep up — keep your hi-hat hand loose so the speed comes from relaxation.

rhythms.name: Funk-Disco / Nu-Disco
rhythms.description: Disco's four-on-the-floor meets funk's 16th-note hats and ghost notes for a slick, busy dance groove, as heard in late-70s funk-disco and its modern nu-disco revival.
rhythms.tip: Keep the kick steady as a metronome while the hands add the funk — the ghost notes should never push the tempo.

rhythms.name: UK Garage 2-Step
rhythms.description: A skippy, shuffled dance groove where the kick avoids beat 3, leaving space for a bouncing swing over the clap backbeat. It is the sound of late-90s London garage.
rhythms.tip: The broken kick is the whole point — never fill in beat 3, and let the swing make the hats skip.

rhythms.name: Gospel 12/8 Ballad
rhythms.description: A slow, soulful church ballad in 12/8 with flowing hi-hat triplets, a deep backbeat and kick pickups that push into beats 1 and 3. Heard behind countless gospel choirs and soul ballads.
rhythms.tip: Lean on the backbeat and let the kick pickups lift the groove forward like a congregation swaying.

rhythms.name: Hambone Clave Beat
rhythms.description: The "shave and a haircut" clave rhythm split between kick (the three side) and snare (the two side). It comes from the hambone body-slap tradition and was made famous on the Bo Diddley records.
rhythms.tip: Clap the clave rhythm first, then play it with kick and snare while the hi-hat keeps straight 8ths.

rhythms.name: Gospel Shuffle
rhythms.description: A bouncy church shuffle with ghost notes between the backbeats, a syncopated kick and an open hi-hat lift on the and of 4.
rhythms.tip: Close the hi-hat right on beat 1 after the open note so the lift snaps back into the groove.

rhythms.name: New Orleans Funk
rhythms.description: A loose, syncopated funk groove with ghost notes and a lazy 16th lilt, rooted in the second-line tradition. Think of Zigaboo Modeliste with The Meters.
rhythms.tip: Let the slight swing pull the 16ths late, and keep the kick syncopations relaxed rather than stiff.

rhythms.name: New Orleans Second Line
rhythms.description: The street parade beat of New Orleans brass bands: a busy, accented snare part over a syncopated bass drum. Drummers like Herlin Riley and Stanton Moore bring it to the drum kit.
rhythms.tip: Make the accents loud and the ghost notes soft so the snare sounds like a marching drummer, not a wall of 16ths.

rhythms.name: Shout / Praise Break
rhythms.description: The high-energy shout groove of Pentecostal churches: kick on every beat with snare on every offbeat, accented on the and of 2 and 4. It drives the "praise break" when the music takes off.
rhythms.tip: Start it slower until the kick-snare alternation is locked, then push the tempo; endurance matters more than speed.

rhythms.name: One Drop
rhythms.description: The classic roots reggae beat: beat 1 is left empty and the kick and cross-stick land together on beat 3, the single heavy "drop".
rhythms.tip: Resist the urge to play a kick on 1; the space on the downbeat is what makes the groove float.

rhythms.name: Ska Upbeat
rhythms.description: Fast, bouncy ska: the hi-hat accents every upbeat to lock with the guitar skank while the snare keeps a backbeat on 2 and 4.
rhythms.tip: Let the hat foot mark the downbeats so the stick hand can lean hard on the "&"s.

rhythms.name: Steppers
rhythms.description: Four-on-the-floor kick with the rimshot still on beat 3; the driving reggae and dub feel that marches forward.
rhythms.tip: Play the kick evenly and not too loud, like a steady heartbeat under the cross-stick on 3.

rhythms.name: Digital Dancehall
rhythms.description: A drum-machine style dancehall pattern: the kick pushes the "&" of 2 and 4 against a hard backbeat and a busy 16th-note hat.
rhythms.tip: Keep the kick pushes on the "&"s short and punchy, and lock them with the bass line.

rhythms.name: Rockers
rhythms.description: Mid-70s rockers style: kick on 1 and 3 under a cross-stick on 3, with busy, syncopated hi-hats and an open-hat bark on the "&" of 4.
rhythms.tip: Keep the ghosted hat notes very soft so the accented 8ths and the open hat jump out.

rhythms.name: Bolero
rhythms.description: The slow, romantic Cuban bolero: steady maracas, the signature cross-stick figure on 2, "&", 4, and open conga tones on 4 and "&". Usually felt over a 2-3 son clave.
rhythms.tip: Play softly and keep the cross-stick figure smooth and singing, it should feel like a slow sway.

rhythms.name: Cha-Cha-Chá
rhythms.description: Relaxed cha-cha-chá: steady quarter-note cowbell, the guiro's long-short-short scrape (on shaker), and the "cha-cha-chá" figure on 4, "&", 1. Usually phrased with a 2-3 son clave.
rhythms.tip: Say "cha-cha-chá" as you play 4, "&", 1; the cross-stick and kick spell it out for the dancers.

rhythms.name: Son Clave & Tumbao (3-2)
rhythms.description: The foundation of salsa and son: 3-2 son clave over the conga tumbao (slap on 2, open tones on 4 and "&") with the kick playing the bass tumbao on "&2" and 4.
rhythms.tip: Count the clave out loud first; once it sits, notice how the kick on beat 4 lines up with the third note of the 3-side.

rhythms.name: Afro-Cuban 6/8 (Bembé)
rhythms.description: The Afro-Cuban 6/8 feel from bembé: the seven-stroke bell pattern rides over four dotted-quarter pulses, with conga slaps and open tones answering.
rhythms.tip: Feel four big beats per bar (count 1 2 3 4 on the dotted quarters) and let the bell float on top.

rhythms.name: Guaguancó Feel (Rumba Clave 3-2)
rhythms.description: A kit-friendly take on Cuban rumba guaguancó: 3-2 rumba clave (third note delayed to the "&" of 4) with palitos on the shell and a simplified two-drum conga conversation.
rhythms.tip: Feel how the rumba clave's late third stroke pulls against the cascara; keep the shell pattern steady and let the congas talk.

rhythms.name: Salsa Cascara (2-3)
rhythms.description: Salsa verse groove in 2-3 son clave: the cascara rhythm on the timbale shell, clave in the left hand, bass-tumbao kick and conga tumbao underneath.
rhythms.tip: On kit, play the cascara on the floor-tom shell or hat with the right hand and the clave as a left-hand cross-stick.

rhythms.name: Songo
rhythms.description: The drum-set-born Cuban groove made famous by Changuito with Los Van Van: quarter-note bell, a ghosted snare melody, and tom notes on 4 and "&" that echo the conga open tones. Implies a 2-3 rumba clave.
rhythms.tip: Practice the left hand (snare and toms) alone until the ghost notes stay quiet, then add the bell on top.

rhythms.name: Ballroom Rhumba
rhythms.description: The slow, sensual rhumba of dance class and ballroom competition: shaker 8ths, cross-stick on 2 and 4, and the habanera-style kick on 1, "&2", 3.
rhythms.tip: The kick on "&2" is the pulse dancers feel; play it lighter than beat 1 but keep it perfectly placed.

rhythms.name: Ballroom Samba
rhythms.description: A simplified samba for the ballroom: shaker 16ths, a cross-stick on each off-beat, and the surdo-style kick "1 . . a 2 . . a" with the heavy note on 2.
rhythms.tip: Make the kick on the second pulse the strongest note in the bar; that low "boom" is what samba dancers bounce to.

rhythms.name: Ballroom Tango
rhythms.description: Staccato, marching ballroom tango: four sharp kicks per bar, a habanera variation in bar 2, and a snare drag that snaps into the next phrase.
rhythms.tip: Keep every note short and crisp, almost clipped; tango is about sharp, dramatic attacks.

rhythms.name: Paso Doble
rhythms.description: The Spanish march of the ballroom: a strong two-beat "oom-pah" with kick on each pulse, snare on the off-beats, and a rolling pickup into the next phrase.
rhythms.tip: Think marching band: proud, even, and steady, with the kick firmly on every pulse.

rhythms.name: Baião
rhythms.description: The northeastern Brazilian baião: the zabumba-style kick on 1 and the "a" of 1 (held through beat 2), with the triangle (shaker) accenting the off-beats.
rhythms.tip: Let the second kick note ring into beat 2 rather than playing on 2; that "dotted" bass figure is the whole groove.

rhythms.name: Bossa Nova
rhythms.description: Gentle bossa nova: straight 8ths on the hat, the two-bar bossa clave on cross-stick (3-side first), and the soft "1 . . & 3 . . &" kick.
rhythms.tip: Play it whisper-quiet; the bossa clave differs from son clave only in the 2-side, where the last note moves to the "&" of 3.

rhythms.name: Samba
rhythms.description: Kit samba in cut time: constant samba 16ths on the ride, the two-bar teleco-teco tamborim phrase on cross-stick, and the surdo kick "1 . . a 2 . . a" with the hat foot on the "&"s.
rhythms.tip: Get the feet going alone first (kick 1-a-2-a, hat foot in between) until they feel automatic, then add the hands.

rhythms.name: Samba-Reggae
rhythms.description: The Afro-Brazilian street-band groove from Salvador, Bahia (popularised by bloco groups like Olodum): a 16th-note snare with clave-shaped accents over a half-time surdo pulse that leans on 2 and 4.
rhythms.tip: Alternate hands on the snare and only play the accents loud; the ghost notes should be barely audible.

rhythms.name: Calypso
rhythms.description: Sunny Trinidadian calypso: hat accents on the off-beats, a light backbeat, and a kick that bounces on 1, "&2", 3, "&4".
rhythms.tip: Accent the "&"s on the hat; the bounce comes from leaning on the off-beats, not the downbeats.

rhythms.name: Cumbia
rhythms.description: Colombian cumbia from the Caribbean coast: the guacharaca's "chk, chi-ki" scrape on shaker, the llamador drum (cross-stick) on every off-beat, and a simple kick on each pulse.
rhythms.tip: The cross-stick on the off-beat is the anchor dancers follow; never rush it.

rhythms.name: Reggaeton (Dembow)
rhythms.description: The dembow rhythm behind reggaeton: kick on every beat with the snare on the "a" of 1 and the "&" of 2, repeated in the second half of the bar (a 3-3-2 tresillo feel).
rhythms.tip: Say "boom-ch-boom-chick" for each half bar; the snare notes always fall just before and just after beat 2 and beat 4.

rhythms.name: Soca
rhythms.description: High-energy carnival soca: four-on-the-floor kick, open hats on every off-beat, and the "iron" (cowbell) chopping "1 . & a" on each beat.
rhythms.tip: Keep the kick rock-steady on every beat; everything else dances around it.

rhythms.name: Merengue
rhythms.description: Fast Dominican merengue in a tight two-beat: the güira (shaker) "long, short-short" pattern, a kick on each pulse, and a kit version of the tambora's rim pickup into an open tone on beat 2.
rhythms.tip: Start at a slower tempo; merengue is played fast, so keep the hands relaxed and low to the drums.

rhythms.name: Highlife
rhythms.description: Joyful West African highlife from Ghana and Nigeria: a clave-like bell timeline over a simple kit pattern of hat 8ths, cross-stick on 2 and 4, and kick on 1 and 3.
rhythms.tip: Learn the bell line by singing it first; the kit part stays simple so the bell and guitars can sparkle.

rhythms.name: Modern Afrobeats
rhythms.description: Contemporary West African pop groove: a lightly swung 16th shaker, rim clicks in a repeating 3-3-2 pattern, claps on 2 and 4, and a laid-back kick.
rhythms.tip: The swing is subtle: let the shaker lilt, but keep the rim and clap notes relaxed and behind the beat.

rhythms.name: Afrobeat
rhythms.description: 1970s Nigerian Afrobeat in the style of Tony Allen: flowing 16th-note hats with open-hat lifts, a ghost-note snare conversation, a sparse syncopated kick, and clave sticks on top.
rhythms.tip: Keep the 16ths on the hat light and continuous, and treat the snare ghosts as quiet chatter around the backbeat.

rhythms.name: West African 12/8 Bell
rhythms.description: The seven-stroke "standard" bell pattern heard across West African music (Ewe dances like agbekor), over a four-pulse kick, shaker, and drum parts that answer the bell.
rhythms.tip: Play the kick on the four dotted-quarter pulses like a dancer's footsteps and feel the bell against it.
